summary: The liquid solver uses genuine particle-fluid techniques, and the scene controls behave as described. Other paths use a grid for gases and surface or volume rendering. The presets and flame colors are tuned graphics effects, without validation as physical material measurements.

claims.claim: The CPU liquid uses density constraints and neighbor velocity smoothing.
claims.how: Kernel constants, isolated gravity motion, and water/honey/lava neighbor smoothing agree with independent calculations. Three constraint iterations approximate a liquid rather than enforce exact volume.

sources.title: Position Based Fluids
sources.says: Position-based density constraints and XSPH velocity smoothing provide a practical particle liquid method for graphics.

claims.note: The tested kernels and smoothing are mathematical checks, not a converged benchmark of the entire solver.

claims.claim: Thickness increases from water to honey and lava in the graphics presets.
claims.how: The stored dimensionless viscosity settings and smoothing passes implement this ordering; they are not measured viscosities of specified materials.

sources.title: Position Based Fluids
sources.says: Position-based density constraints and XSPH velocity smoothing provide a practical particle liquid method for graphics.

claims.claim: The listed GPU material viscosities are verified real-world values.
claims.how: The code labels water 0.000001, honey 0.004, and lava 0.01 as m²/s, then applies a floor and a time-step cap. No temperature, composition, density source, or experimental reference is supplied.
claims.note: The particle-fluid and graphics references were inspected; neither verifies these material values. A physical-data source and stated conditions are still needed.

claims.claim: The scene controls pour, drain, splash, extinguish, and blow.
claims.how: The actual recipe outputs activate pouring, drain on the third glass tap, extinguish and restart the candle, and add wind across the cup.

sources.title: Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids
sources.publisher: Crane, Llamas, and Tariq, GPU Gems 3, NVIDIA
sources.says: Grid fluid animation uses advection, buoyancy, pressure projection, and vorticity confinement, with volume rendering for smoke and fire.

claims.claim: Gas and flame motion represent graphics effects.
claims.how: The CPU curl field is divergence-free at checked points, but buoyancy, lifetimes, spreading, and flame colors are prescribed. The GPU path instead advects gas on a grid.

sources.title: Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids
sources.publisher: Crane, Llamas, and Tariq, GPU Gems 3, NVIDIA
sources.says: Grid fluid animation uses advection, buoyancy, pressure projection, and vorticity confinement, with volume rendering for smoke and fire.

claims.note: No chemical combustion or measured temperature-to-color relation is established by these checks.

claims.claim: Flows can be rendered as particles, liquid surfaces, or gas volumes.
claims.how: The original all-particles description was too broad: the GPU gas path stores grid fields and renders volumes. The description now distinguishes particles and grids without assuming all gases or flames are particles.

simplified: The CPU liquid uses position-based density constraints and velocity smoothing; the GPU liquid uses a different grid-particle method. Smoke and flame may use a grid or prescribed particles. Foam, bubbles, heat, colors, and thickness are tuned effects. Numerical checks here do not establish measured volume conservation, temperature, or material accuracy.

fixes.what: Replace the all-particles description with a statement that gases can use a grid, depending on the rendering path.

Treat the GPU viscosity table as tuned presets unless authoritative material data, temperature, units, and calibration tests are supplied. Add mass, density, and convergence benchmarks before scientific accuracy claims.
